data.turoyo: ʕAmmo Išoʕ: Ak kurmanǧ ste aṯənwo, hanək ste mḥayaffe aʕle ġalabe. <...>
data.translation: Uncle Isho: The Kurds too had come; they too mourned him greatly. <...>

rationale: Thin II.1 Preterit cell; plural mourners and ʕal-target, one example for the verse's repeated predicate. English is the supplied project machine translation.

data.turoyo: <...> E, du šrolo kayiwo we, bas mḥayafno ġalabe, qay lo m meqəm qadərno d ḥuzenole. <...>
data.translation: <...> Yes, he truly was ill, but I regret very much that I had not been able to see him earlier. <...>

rationale: Thin II.1 Infectum cell; first-person experiencer with the regretted content expressed in a qay-clause. English is the supplied project machine translation.

summary: Both supplied occurrences fit inherited II.1 bedauern, bejammern. The 6/22 and 30/138 contexts are already the two Infectum examples; neither is printed again.

In 6/22 the experiencer u babo is the ordinary subject; ʕal hayo supplies the cause/topic of lamenting. The later ʕal qarʕe d ruḥe belongs to coordinated gmoḥe and must not be assigned as another complement of kəmḥayəf.
30/138 has plural experiencers in kəmḥayfi; the following wish supplies the regretted situation. Narrative past time in the edition does not change the kə-marked form’s Infectum classification.

The inherited etymology compares a Turoyo nominal expression, Arabic ḥayf ʕalayhi and Kurdish heyf lêhatin. The occurrences attest an inflected Stem II verb; they do not choose between contact sources or demonstrate a separate light-verb construction.
The inherited note with komətḥayafno is retained verbatim as unstructured draft material; neither present occurrence establishes its Detransitive status or relation to another entry.
Plural mḥayaffe has the experiencer as agent-suffixed subject and the lamented person in aʕle. Infectum mḥayafno instead expresses regret with a reason/content clause.
Round 1 adds no examples or senses for this root. The new contexts fill existing thin boxes and do not settle Arabic-versus-Kurdish contact history or the tḥyf relationship.
